item.title: EA is shutting down BioWare (437 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theverge.com/games/1015647/ea-is-shutting-down-bioware, See on Hacker News

BioWare, the legendary studio behind RPGs like Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, is shutting down, the company confirmed in a statement. Alongside the closure, Electronic Arts has chosen not to continue development on the next Mass Effect game that was in the works, according to an announcement sent to EA staff.

The company is also laying off around 400 staffers, Bloomberg reports, including around 50 at BioWare. The changes follow EA being taken private by an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners in a $55 billion deal that closed in August. Other major gaming companies have made sweeping changes this year as well, including Xbox’s “reset” that will include 3,200 cuts, Bungie’s “significant” layoffs, and Fortnite maker Epic Games laying off over 1,000 staff.

“BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly,” Cam Weber, EA president and chief studios officer, and David Tinson, EA president and COO, said in the announcement.

For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life.

Baldur’s Gate. Neverwinter Nights. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. Dragon Age. Mass Effect. Anthem.

Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending.

There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition.

What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own.

From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.

While the end of BioWare will shock many gamers who fondly remember its hits, the company hasn’t been as successful in recent years. 2017’s Mass Effect: Andromeda was widely seen as a misstep for that franchise, it took a big bet on live service games in 2019 with Anthem that didn’t pan out, and EA laid off some BioWare staff in 2025 after Dragon Age: The Veilguard missed sales expectations.

There is no word yet on the fate of Amazon’s Mass Effect TV series. Last we heard, Amazon’s head of TV was close to giving it the green light, but had reportedly requested rewrites to make the show “more appealing to non-gamers.” Amazon didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. EA spokesperson Justin Higgs said he had “Nothing to share on that at this point.”

In EA’s company-wide announcement, Weber and Tinson outlined several other projects in development and changes to EA’s roadmap. The executives say that Respawn and DICE will be collaborating on “a future project,” which Bloomberg says is “likely” a new Star Wars: Battlefront game. The company is still working Marvel’s Iron Man and a new Star Wars Jedi title. EA is making a “brand-new, social-first open-world experience” football game that it calls “Project Gridiron” and is also in pre-production on a new Fight Night boxing title (which was teased yesterday). For The Sims, the company is pausing development on “Project Lotus” and focusing on “Project Evergreen.” And for its live-service Skate, EA is “making changes to the studio” to “deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community.”

Hi Team,

First, thank you.

Through every major moment we’ve faced as a company, your commitment to creating awesome games and experiences for our players continues to be impressive. Together, we’ve built epic worlds and global communities that are part of the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest.

That’s why, over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business, how we operate, and what it will take to lead in this next era of interactive entertainment. We’ve challenged assumptions, confronted hard realities, imagined new possibilities, and made deliberate choices in order to deliver exceptional experiences for our players and to drive sustained growth.

We believe our best creative work happens when we’re clear about what matters most for our players and give our teams the freedom to move quickly. So, we’re concentrating our teams, technology, and investment behind these three strategic priorities.

These priorities will bring clarity and focus to your work every day, and so will the way we work. We’ve spent time listening to teams about what’s working, what’s getting in the way, and what you need to do your best work. The feedback was consistent: you want clearer priorities, faster decisions, and teams that work more closely together. We’ve already begun simplifying how we work so we can spend more time creating and innovating for our players.

Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth.

In our Shooters business, Battlefield 6 was a great success, and we learned a lot from the launch and the live service. We’re going to take those learnings, balance our resources, and leverage the technology to deliver a shooter portfolio that unlocks growth. In addition to our future Battlefield titles, we’ll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project that will help us achieve that ambition. We can’t wait to share more when the time comes. We’re also continuing to invest heavily in Apex over the next few years by introducing brand new gameplay modes in multiplayer, and other new experiences, to expand the universe.

Action-adventure is one of the most competitive and high-stakes genres in the industry, where every game needs our full weight behind it. We’re continuing to deliver on our two huge launches coming up with Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game. Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success.

As we focus on these larger opportunities, we’ve had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect. We’ve made the decision not to move forward with this development, which means we’re closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace. BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly.

EA SPORTS continues to operate from a position of strength. We are fully committed and investing in the global growth of our FC franchise and across the full EA SPORTS portfolio. We have two new projects in development you’ll hear about over the next few months, including a brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call “Project Gridiron,” and we are also in pre-production to bring back a beloved, fan-favorite in Fight Night, leveraging capabilities from our simulation fighting team.

In Lifestyle, we’re focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims and skate. We’re going to prioritize our efforts on “Project Evergreen” for The Sims to give the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game, and to help make this possible, we’re pausing development on “Project Lotus.” For skate., we’ve had a lot of success in bringing players into the game, and we need to create an experience that keeps them engaged over the long-term. To do that, we are making changes to the studio to have a more focused, smaller team to deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community that we believe will build a healthier and more sustainable business.

The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we’re committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect.

We’re sure there will be questions about what these changes mean for individual teams and for EA more broadly. You can speak directly with your leaders to hear more on that, and we’ll make sure to spend time discussing our direction and the work ahead at our next Global Town Hall in November.

The past several months have strengthened our belief in what EA can become. We have extraordinary people, franchises that matter to millions of players, and opportunities to build experiences we’ve only begun to imagine.

Our responsibility is to make the choices, provide the clarity, and create the conditions for our teams to do their best work. We also want to give every game we choose to build its best chance to succeed for our players and fans around the world.

We look forward to building more great games and experiences together.

Thanks,

Cam & David

item.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security (578 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/, See on Hacker News

Earlier today, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. These releases fix two critical vulnerabilities that, under the right conditions, allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems.

This post isn't about how to update. It's about how these vulnerabilities were found and fixed, what has changed in how PHP security is handled over the past two years, and what we need from the organizations that depend on PHP to keep PHP's security work going.

  • CVE-2026-109618 / GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w: RCE via OOM corruption (out-of-memory): If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory. On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs, and full remote code execution was demonstrated with default settings. Remote code execution was also confirmed on PHP-FPM through application-level code paths.
  • CVE-2026-109619 / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp: RCE via stale state: A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request. A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.

Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling. Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions.

A first external audit and increased security focus

In 2024, PHP underwent its first external security audit in years. The PHP Foundation secured funding from the Sovereign Tech Agency to organize this audit through OSTIF, and it was carried out by Quarkslab. While fixing one of the issues Quarkslab reported, a PHP core developer contracted by the PHP Foundation found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618. In 2024, a potential exploit for the OOM problem was theorized, but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.

To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs: backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources. The security team has since started changing its processes, and that work continues, so that decisions can be made by majority and compromises are encouraged.

Building a sustainable professional security organization

Over the last months the way PHP security work is organized has changed considerably. In May 2026, the PHP Foundation created the Ecosystem Security Team, which works alongside the PHP security team on triage, coordination, and hardening. Volker Dusch's work as AI Security Engineer in Residence at the PHP Foundation has significantly improved communication and collaboration between the PHP security team and the Foundation. Alexandre Daubois joined the PHP Foundation in July to help the PHP security team triage, handle, and fix security reports and Daniel Scherzer joined in September to take on hardening work.

Earlier this year, we worked with Alpha-Omega to scan PHP with Anthropic's Claude Mythos. But since the Mythos scan, we have added other tools, including OpenAI's Daybreak Red for validating reports and exploits, alongside sanitizer builds and reproduction environments that match our CI on every platform PHP supports.

The PHP Foundation got the PHP project into the Patch the Planet program, as part of which security firm Calif began an audit of PHP on July 30th, 2026. On August 11th researcher Ryan A at Calif reported an unconditional remote code execution with the same root cause as the OOM problem we had found in 2024. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause on the same day, followed by further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th. More recently, Trail of Bits has also been auditing PHP. The reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz made the full impact of the OOM problem clear, and from August 11th onward, fixing it became the top priority for all of the PHP Foundation's team working on security. Without the Foundation’s funding it would have been impossible to have multiple people work on this issue full time, eventually through weekends and around the clock to coordinate and communicate with other involved parties.

The growth of AI-assisted research also means the PHP security team receives far more reports than before. As Alexandre Daubois described last week in How the PHP Security Team Handles Your Reports, the team has published 15 CVEs since July 1st and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible. AI helps the team validate reports and group reports sharing the same root cause, but a person makes every call and works on every patch.

Leak and disrupted disclosure

The coordinated disclosure of these vulnerabilities worked well until 2 days ahead of the targeted release date.

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC. Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update. Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.

As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.

Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well. The PHP security team closely monitored and inspected appearing PoCs after the leak but did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.

On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.

A cautiously optimistic outlook

Today's release shows the progress we’re making in how PHP security is handled. Once the full impact of the OOM problem was understood in August, the security team, the foundation, and the release managers delivered a fix for this deeply rooted problem across all supported branches, and distributions and LTS vendors received the patch ahead of time so their users can update quickly.

We are confident that a serious vulnerability with a fix stuck on hard trade-offs would now reach the PHP Foundation leadership much sooner, as we’re changing processes so leadership can help steer the situation to a timely resolution. We are now prioritizing measures to make sure vulnerabilities that need similarly complex fixes get resolved faster when they are reported in the future. The PHP Foundation and the PHP security team learned a lot in the last weeks and will work to turn their experiences into lasting repeatable processes.

What we need from you

PHP runs a large share of the web, including government services, online stores, banks, media sites, and much of the software that businesses rely on every day. Yet security work on PHP itself still depends on a small group of foundation-funded developers and a little volunteer help.

Tools now find bugs faster than ever, for defenders and attackers alike, and the number of reports will keep growing. What tools cannot do is decide on the right fix for a long-standing design decision in the engine, weigh the compatibility trade-offs, and review the patch. Making those decisions takes experienced engineers who know the entire PHP codebase, and today there are too few of them.

A core part of the PHP Foundation's mission is to grow the number of engineers with deep knowledge of the PHP codebase and give the security team the resources it needs. We can only achieve this goal with funding from those who depend on PHP:

  • Companies that build products and services on PHP: please sponsor the PHP Foundation at a level that reflects how much you rely on it.
  • Hosting providers, cloud platforms, and distributions that deliver PHP to millions of users.
  • Governments and public institutions whose services run on PHP. The German Sovereign Tech Agency's funding of the 2024 audit shows what public investment can achieve, and we need more of it, on a sustained basis.

Sponsoring the PHP Foundation is the most direct way to ensure structural issues like the OOM vulnerability are addressed sustainably, before they turn into emergencies. Become a sponsor at thephp.foundation/sponsor, and if your organization would like to talk about a larger commitment, get in touch.

Thank you

Thank you to the PHP security team, volunteers and PHP Foundation contractors alike, the release managers, and the package maintainers at distributions and LTS vendors who made these releases possible. Thank you to Calif, especially Ryan A, Wiz, OpenAI Codex Security, especially Amy Burnett, OSTIF, and Quarkslab for their research and responsible disclosure; to Alpha-Omega, OpenAI, and Anthropic for giving the team access to their tools and funding some of the security work; to the Sovereign Tech Agency for funding the 2024 audit; and to all of our sponsors, whose support made this work possible.

item.title: DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS "Cinnamon Teal" (339 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://duckdb.org/2026/10/21/announcing-duckdb-200, See on Hacker News

Blog Release

TL;DR: The DuckDB team is happy to announce that today we're releasing DuckDB version 2.0.0 LTS, codenamed “Cinnamon Teal” (Spatula cyanoptera). This is our biggest feature release so far, and it ships a polished version of the Quack protocol, asynchronous I/O, a first-class VARIANT type, agent mode, triggers, an extensible SQL parser and much more, built from close to 20,000 commits since DuckDB 1.5.

We are proud to release DuckDB 2.0.0, codenamed “Cinnamon Teal” after the Spatula cyanoptera, a strikingly reddish-brown duck found in the western Americas.

While DuckDB 1.0 was all about stability and backward compatibility, DuckDB 2.0 is above all a feature release. In this blog post, we summarize the highlights and then walk through the breaking changes and how to migrate. We showcased many of the new features in “A Preview of DuckDB v2.0”, which covers each one in more depth. For the complete release notes, see the release page on GitHub.

Tip To install the new version, please visit the installation page. Some clients, such as the CLI and Python, are already available. Other client libraries (e.g., Go, R, Java) and some extensions can take a few days to release due to the extra changes and review rounds required.

With this release, there are currently three DuckDB lines available. DuckDB 2.0 is a long-term support (LTS) release with support until at least October 2027. The previous LTS release, version 1.4, is still supported until late November 2026. To ensure a smooth transition and allow sufficient time for testing, we extended the support period of DuckDB 1.5 until March 2027, effectively also turning it into an LTS release. For details, see the release calendar.

To find your way around the documentation for all of the new features, we also published a “What's New in the Docs for 2.0” page that links each feature below to its documentation.

DuckDB as a Server

DuckDB has been an in-process database since day one. In DuckDB 1.5.3, released in May, we introduced the Quack protocol that lets you run DuckDB in a traditional client-server setup, along with the quack extension, which implements DuckDB's native protocol, so any DuckDB process can serve its databases.

Quack and CONNECT

DuckDB 2.0.0 ships a polished version of the Quack protocol with substantial performance and stability improvements. It also introduces the new CONNECT statement that allows attaching and switching to a remote database in a single command for better ergonomics:

DuckDB server 

CALL quack_serve(
    token = 'my_token'
);

CREATE TABLE events
    (date DATE, name VARCHAR);

INSERT INTO events VALUES
    ('2027-04-07',
     'DuckCon #8');

quack:

DuckDB client 

ATTACH 'quack:localhost'
    AS qk (TOKEN 'my_token');

CONNECT qk;
SELECT * FROM events;

┌────────────┬────────────┐
│    date    │    name    │
│    date    │  varchar   │
├────────────┼────────────┤
│ 2027-04-07 │ DuckCon #8 │
└────────────┴────────────┘

For simplicity, this example runs the server and the client on the same machine. By default, the server only listens on localhost. To accept connections from other machines, keep the server on localhost and put it behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. The allow_other_hostname option, which exposes the server directly, is only meant for testing.

The CONNECT statement is not limited to Quack: it points your session at any remote database that supports it, including PostgreSQL and MySQL. For these, the new remote pushdown optimizer ships queries directly to the remote server instead of pulling tables over the wire.

Quack in the CLI

The CLI also has shortcuts for setting up a Quack client-server pair: the new -serve and -connect arguments start a Quack server or connect to one directly from the command line:

CLI server 

CREATE TABLE t AS
      SELECT 42 AS x;

quack:

CLI client 

FROM t;

┌───────┐
│   x   │
│ int32 │
├───────┤
│    42 │
└───────┘

Performance

Asynchronous I/O

DuckDB 2.0 introduces asynchronous I/O for reading Parquet and CSV files. The I/O layer now scales independently from the query processing layer, issuing reads in the background and keeping multiple requests in flight. This means far more parallelism for remote reads and dramatically faster queries on object storage such as s3://.

We described the design in detail in a dedicated blog post. In that post, we showed the network throughput over the course of a query with and without asynchronous I/O:

Network throughput. Higher utilization and shorter runtime are better.

The VARIANT Type Becomes a First-Class Citizen

The VARIANT type stores semi-structured, schema-less data such as JSON while keeping the performance of columnar execution. So you can think of it as JSON on steroids: a VARIANT column can store differently shaped data in every row, but unlike JSON it is not a text format.

DuckDB 1.5 already introduced VARIANT, but DuckDB 2.0 fully integrates it. DuckDB 2.0 detects the common structure in your data and “shreds” it, so it compresses well and executes fast. The pipeline works end to end, from shredded execution straight out of storage to shredded VARIANT reading and writing for Parquet, backed by a family of variant_* functions. For example:

CREATE TABLE events (payload VARIANT);
INSERT INTO events
VALUES
    ('{"user": {"id": 42, "tags": ["a", "b"]}}'::JSON::VARIANT),
    ('{"event": "click", "x": 10, "y": 20}'::JSON::VARIANT);

SELECT variant_type(payload), variant_keys(payload)
FROM events;

┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│ variant_type(payload) │ variant_keys(payload) │
│        varchar        │       varchar[]       │
├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│ OBJECT                │ [user]                │
│ OBJECT                │ [event, x, y]         │
└───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

Agent Mode in the CLI

Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor increasingly drive the DuckDB CLI on their users' behalf. The 2.0 CLI detects when it is being run by an agent and switches to agent mode: it prints compact Markdown tables instead of padded boxes, says clearly when a result was truncated, stops runaway queries early and reports errors as JSON.

Long-running SQL queries report their expected cost prior to running, so the agent can decide whether to wait. In our experiments on TPC-H, agent mode cut the amount of DuckDB output the model had to read by 59%. You can turn it on for manual testing using the -agent flag or instruct your agent to turn it off using the -no-agent flag.

Extensibility

A Brand New SQL Parser

DuckDB has always used a parser derived from PostgreSQL's. In 2.0, our own modern, extensible PEG-based parser, which debuted as an opt-in feature in DuckDB 1.5, becomes the default. Extensions can now hook into the grammar itself (an idea we first explored in our research on runtime-extensible parsers), so expect extensions that expose entirely new SQL syntax. Error messages now come with precise source locations. For details, see the PEG parser documentation. The new parser is designed to be compatible with the old one, so you should not notice the swap. If you do, please file an issue. In the meantime, you can switch back to the old parser using the legacy_parser extension by running SET enable_legacy_parser = true;.

The old parser had served DuckDB since its first commit in 2018. Its grammar was generated with YACC/Bison, which produces an LALR(1) parser, so as DuckSQL grew, even small additions could collide with existing rules and raise shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflicts. A PEG grammar avoids this by trying alternatives in the order they are written, so adding syntax no longer risks breaking unrelated rules. Python itself moved to a PEG-based parser in version 3.9 for the same flexibility.

Write Extensions Once and Host Them Yourself

DuckDB 2.0 ships a revamped C API v2, which is considerably more powerful than its predecessor and exposes components such as file systems and table functions to extensions. Before marking it as stable, we would like to test it in the field, so please give it a try and send us your feedback!

You can also register and host your own trusted extension repositories, so an organization can host and sign its own extensions and have them install and load just like the built-in ones:

SET allow_extension_repositories = 'allowed';

CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY my_repo
    WITH PREFIX 'https://extensions.example.org';

INSTALL AND LOAD my_ext FROM my_repo;

A repository is a name, a URL prefix and one or more RSA public keys that are trusted to sign the extensions served from it. The prefix can point at anything DuckDB can read: a local path, https, s3, you name it. At CREATE time, DuckDB fetches the repository's public keys and pins them into the repository definition, printing each key's SHA-256 fingerprint so you can compare it against one published out of band.

This feature is still a work in progress and its syntax may change in future releases. For more details, see the Extension Repositories page.

Core Extension Updates

DuckDB's core extensions are also shipping several new features, fixes and performance optimizations. These are too numerous to all list here, so we only highlight a few of them and will cover them in dedicated blog posts in the coming weeks:

  • We released DuckLake 1.1, including a new specification and reference implementation.
  • The Iceberg extension strives to become a feature-complete implementation. To this end, it adds REST catalog ATTACH options that derive a table's location from its namespace or load table metadata from the metadata-location file returned by the catalog. Further options control the URL prefix and the namespace separator.
  • The Delta extension can create Delta tables with CREATE TABLE (including partitioning and Delta table properties), supports time travel and improves VARIANT support.

SQL Features

Triggers

DuckDB 2.0 delivers triggers: the CREATE TRIGGER statement with BEFORE and AFTER triggers, FOR EACH ROW and FOR EACH STATEMENT, transition tables via REFERENCING OLD/NEW TABLE, multiple triggers per event, RETURNING on triggered tables and DROP TRIGGER. The classic use case is audit tables, where a trigger records what changed in response to a table modification. Some combinations, such as BEFORE ... FOR EACH ROW and UPDATE ... FOR EACH ROW triggers, are not yet supported; see the limitations.

CREATE TRIGGER trg_audit
    AFTER UPDATE ON target
    REFERENCING
        OLD TABLE AS o
        NEW TABLE AS n
    FOR EACH STATEMENT
        INSERT INTO audit
        SELECT n.id, o.val, n.val
        FROM o JOIN n ON o.id = n.id;

Triggers can also maintain materialized views incrementally! For example, to keep track of the average age of people per nationality in a table age_statistics, you can use two triggers – one for insert and another for delete operations – and store the sum and the count alongside the average.

To see more details, click here. 
CREATE TABLE people (name VARCHAR, nationality VARCHAR, age INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE age_statistics (
    nationality VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY,
    sum_age INTEGER,
    num_people INTEGER,
    average_age DOUBLE
);

On insertion, we aggregate the new rows per nationality and merge them into age_statistics, adding a row for each new nationality:

CREATE TRIGGER people_insert
    AFTER INSERT ON people
    REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n
    FOR EACH STATEMENT
        MERGE INTO age_statistics s
        USING (
            SELECT nationality, sum(age) AS sum_age, count(*) AS num_people
            FROM n
            GROUP BY nationality
        ) d
        ON s.nationality = d.nationality
        WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
            sum_age = s.sum_age + d.sum_age,
            num_people = s.num_people + d.num_people,
            average_age = (s.sum_age + d.sum_age) / (s.num_people + d.num_people)
        WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
            VALUES (d.nationality, d.sum_age, d.num_people, d.sum_age / d.num_people);

On deletion, we subtract the deleted rows and drop a nationality once its last person has left:

CREATE TRIGGER people_delete
    AFTER DELETE ON people
    REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS o
    FOR EACH STATEMENT
        MERGE INTO age_statistics s
        USING (
            SELECT nationality, sum(age) AS sum_age, count(*) AS num_people
            FROM o
            GROUP BY nationality
        ) d
        ON s.nationality = d.nationality
        WHEN MATCHED AND s.num_people = d.num_people THEN DELETE
        WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET
            sum_age = s.sum_age - d.sum_age,
            num_people = s.num_people - d.num_people,
            average_age = (s.sum_age - d.sum_age) / (s.num_people - d.num_people);

Let's see people come and go:

INSERT INTO people VALUES
    ('Alice', 'US', 34), ('Bram', 'NL', 27), ('Csilla', 'HU', 45),
    ('Dave', 'US', 58), ('Eva', 'NL', 19), ('Femke', 'NL', 41);
FROM age_statistics ORDER BY nationality;

┌─────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
│ nationality │ sum_age │ num_people │ average_age │
│   varchar   │  int32  │   int32    │   double    │
├─────────────┼─────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
│ HU          │      45 │          1 │        45.0 │
│ NL          │      87 │          3 │        29.0 │
│ US          │      92 │          2 │        46.0 │
└─────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

DELETE FROM people WHERE name = 'Alice';
DELETE FROM people WHERE nationality = 'HU';
FROM age_statistics ORDER BY nationality;

┌─────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
│ nationality │ sum_age │ num_people │ average_age │
│   varchar   │  int32  │   int32    │   double    │
├─────────────┼─────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
│ NL          │      87 │          3 │        29.0 │
│ US          │      58 │          1 │        58.0 │
└─────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

Triggers bring us one step closer to materialized views, a long-standing item in the “future work” section of our roadmap.

SQL Dialect Additions

As always, DuckDB's friendly SQL dialect keeps growing. A few favorites from this release cycle:

  • The $variable shorthand lets you write $x in most places where an expression is allowed, instead of getvariable('x').
  • Data-modifying CTEs let you use INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and COPY as pipeline steps.
  • NEAREST joins turn top-k similarity search into a join clause, handy for vector and embedding workloads.
  • Nested schemas allow schemas within schemas, e.g., CREATE SCHEMA finance.reports.
  • JSON mutation functions json_set, json_insert, json_replace and json_remove return modified copies of JSON documents (see also our blog post on JSON patches).

There is more: DuckDB 2.0.0 supports the SQL-standard FETCH FIRST and allows UNNEST in the GROUP BY clause. It also ensures well-defined MERGE and UPDATE ... FROM semantics for cases when multiple rows are matched.

Migrating to 2.0

DuckDB 2.0 comes with a small set of breaking changes. For most users, upgrading is straightforward, but complex deployments running many DuckDB processes need more care. The storage format is the most likely source of problems: DuckDB versions before 2.0 cannot read database files created by DuckDB 2.0. DuckDB 2.0 can still read and write your existing database files, and these remain readable by older versions. We recommend testing 2.0.0 on a shadow system before switching production over. And, if your workload is mission-critical, you may want to wait for the first patch release, coming in November.

For the full details, see the migration guide.

Internals and Deprecations

Compiler Requirements

Following DuckDB's long stint on C++11, DuckDB 2.0 now requires a C++17 compiler.

We also switched to Clang as the default compiler for our release builds. On Linux and macOS, both DuckDB and its core extensions are built with Clang. On Windows, the CLI is built with Clang, while most core extensions are still built with MSVC. We may move more Windows builds to Clang in the future, but this requires further changes.

Timezones, Calendars and Collations Without ICU

Timezone-aware timestamps, calendars and collations have always been powered by the ICU library. In 2.0, the ICU library is gone entirely: the icu extension now implements timezones, calendars and collations itself, with the timezone data built directly from the IANA database and compressed down to around 45 kB.

Everything keeps working exactly as before, and the native implementation is also faster. If you find any issues, please let us know!

Deprecations

Lambda Syntax

The old single-arrow lambda syntax (x -> x + 1) is now disabled by default. Use the Python-style syntax instead:

SELECT list_transform([1, 2, 3], lambda x: x + 1);

You can temporarily re-enable the old syntax with SET lambda_syntax = 'enable_single_arrow';. Both the flag and the single-arrow syntax will be removed entirely in v2.1.

Amalgamation Builds

The amalgamation build, which bundles DuckDB's entire source code into a single header and a single source file, is now deprecated. The amalgamation has grown too large to be realistically useful in most cases.

Gradual Phase-Out of macOS x86_64

We are gradually phasing out osx_amd64 from the list of fully supported platforms. For the time being, DuckDB and core extensions are still built and supported, but community extensions are no longer built for this platform. DuckDB 2.1 will stop supporting osx_amd64.

Summary

These were a few highlights, but there are many more features and improvements in this release. There have been almost 20,000 commits by many contributors since DuckDB 1.5, shipping smaller features as well as performance and usability improvements. The full release notes can be found on GitHub.

We would like to thank our community for the detailed issue reports and feedback that have driven this release, and our special thanks go to our contributors!

item.title: Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI Installs a Credential Stealer and Backdoor (372 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://safedep.io/litellm-pypi-compromise-credential-stealer-backdoor/, See on Hacker News

• Oct 21, 2026 • 6 min read

The LiteLLM 1.107.0 release on PyPI carries a credential stealer and a remote code execution backdoor. All seven wheels (Linux, macOS, Windows) install them as three files in site-packages. Both run when any Python process starts on the host, even one that never imports litellm. The upstream GitHub source does not contain them. PyPI has since removed the release.

Versions 1.106.2, 1.107.0rc1, and 1.107.0rc2 are clean. The companion packages that 1.107.0 pins, litellm-proxy-extras==0.4.110 and litellm-enterprise==0.1.78, are also clean.

What the attack does

Installing litellm==1.107.0 places three files in site-packages. Python loads two of them each time it starts.

  1. cook.pth imports cook.py, a credential stealer. It collects SSH keys, cloud credentials, CI/CD secrets, AI tool tokens, browser passwords, and the LLM provider keys in a LiteLLM proxy database. It encrypts the data and sends it to www.litellm[.]dev.
  2. sitecustomize.py starts a background daemon. Every hour, the daemon reads a server address from a GitHub file, runs the stealer again, and downloads and runs code from that server.

How the implant got into the release

The pyproject.toml in the 1.107.0 source distribution (sdist) has one extra line in the maturin build section:

pyproject.toml (litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz)

TOML 6 lines

The maturin data = "cook" setting copies a cook/ folder into litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/ in the wheel. pip installs that folder into site-packages.

The sdist leaves out the cook/ folder, so this line is the only visible change. No public commit in BerriAI/litellm contains data = "cook" or a cook/ folder.

The wheel RECORD lists the three added files:

litellm-1.107.0.dist-info/RECORD

TEXT 4 lines

The release does not match its tag

The tag v1.107.0 points to commit 66c8f5b (06:59 UTC). Its pyproject.toml says version = "1.108.0". SafeDep compared every sdist file with the git trees by blob hash. The sdist matches a later main commit, a8113b0 (08:50 UTC), plus five edited files and the cook/ folder.

Four of the edited files are Cargo.toml files that gain a readme = "README.md" line. The legitimate 1.106.2 and rc2 releases have the same edit. The fifth is pyproject.toml, compared here with a8113b0:

pyproject.toml (a8113b0 → litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz)

DIFF 11 lines

The edit sets the version back to 1.107.0 and pins the companion packages to the rc2 values. As a result, a dependency diff against rc2 shows nothing unusual. The legitimate 1.106.2 sdist matches its tag commit 49943cd except for the Cargo.toml readme lines.

How the wheels were built

The malicious wheels match the output of the normal BerriAI release pipeline:

  • The WHEEL file names maturin 1.9.4, the same version as in the legitimate releases. The implant files have correct RECORD entries, which shows no edits after the build.
  • Zip timestamps show separate native builds: macOS at 11:20, Linux at 11:21, and Windows at 11:37 UTC.
  • In the Windows wheel, all 2,804 .py files have CRLF line endings, including the three implant files. The Linux wheel has none. A git checkout on Windows with line-ending conversion produces this pattern.

No public GitHub Actions run built or published the release. SafeDep checked all 539 runs between 09:30 and 12:30 UTC. At 11:50 UTC, about 10 minutes after the PyPI upload, litellm-dispatcher[bot] published the GitHub release v1.107.0. The same delay occurred for 1.106.2. PyPI has no provenance attestations for 1.107.0, 1.106.2, or rc2.

SafeDep assesses, with moderate to high confidence, that BerriAI’s private release pipeline built these wheels from an attacker-modified git source. The attacker could have used a compromised maintainer or bot credential, a private branch or mirror, or the reference the pipeline builds from. A stolen PyPI token used from the attacker’s own machines fits the evidence less well. Only BerriAI’s pipeline logs can confirm the cause.

Payload 1: the credential stealer in cook.py

At startup, Python runs each line that starts with import in a .pth file in site-packages. cook.pth contains import cook, so the stealer runs in every Python process on the host: the application, pip, IDE language servers, and CI jobs.

cook.py wraps about 61 KB of Python in one layer of exec(zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode('...'))). The decoded code starts with this configuration:

What it collects

ModuleTargets
sysinfo, netinfoHost name, user, operating system, IP addresses, network settings
browser_pwChromium saved passwords, decrypted with the profile master key (DPAPI on Windows). Firefox logins.json and key4.db
browser_histBrowser history
ssh_keys~/.ssh/*
shell_histbash and zsh history, PowerShell PSReadLine, cmd history
cloud_creds~/.aws/credentials and config, Azure profile and tokens, gcloud credentials, ~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json, gh hosts.yml, rclone.conf, ~/.netrc
dev_secrets.pem, .key, .pfx, .p12, .pk8, .ppk files under $HOME, Composer auth.json, FileZilla saved servers
container_credsKubernetes service account token
cicd_secretsGitLab runner config.toml, Jenkins initialAdminPassword and master.key, .vault-token, Terraform credentials.tfrc.json, Packer settings
ai_devtoolsClaude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, VS Code mcp.json, Gemini CLI, Codex auth.json, Continue, Aider, Goose, opencode, Qwen, Crush, Kiro, Zed, Hugging Face token
env_varsIts own environment and the environment of other processes through /proc/<pid>/environ
db_litellmReads DATABASE_URL and dumps the LiteLLM_CredentialsTable and LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable tables, which hold the LLM provider API keys of a LiteLLM proxy
cloud_metadataAWS instance metadata service (IMDSv2, then v1): instance identity and role credentials
gpg_keys, tls_privkeyGPG keys, TLS private keys

How it sends the data

  1. It encrypts the JSON results with a random AES-256-CBC key, and encrypts that key with RSA-OAEP and the embedded public key.
  2. It packs the result into a tar.gz (hdr.json, data.bin, key.bin) and sends it in a POST request to www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck with the header X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb.
  3. After a successful upload, it writes /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb so it collects only once per host. It also sets PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE=1 to avoid a second run in the same process tree.

Payload 2: the backdoor in sitecustomize.py

Python imports sitecustomize at startup, so this file also runs in every Python process.

  1. It takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock, so only one daemon runs per host.
  2. It calls fork() and setsid(), sends standard input and output to /dev/null, and changes directory to / to detach from the parent process.
  3. Every hour, it:
    1. reads domain.txt from the attacker’s GitHub repository and takes the first line that looks like a domain,
    2. runs its embedded copy of the stealer, which has no once-per-host marker,
    3. downloads http://<domain>/codepy and runs it with exec().

The attacker can point the daemon at a new server by editing domain.txt. Each infected host runs whatever that server returns as codepy.

At 13:40 UTC, the GitHub account letters9813 and its repository returned 404, about two hours after the release. The backdoor now finds no server address and does nothing. Hosts that ran the daemon before the deletion could have received and run second-stage code. SafeDep could not recover the server address.

item.description:
URL: https://www.php.net/index.php, See on Hacker News

21 Oct 2026

Security advisory: Critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, update now

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately.

Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.

The vulnerabilities:

  • RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.
  • RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

How to update:

  • Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Source downloads are on our downloads page. Windows source and binaries are on the same page.
  • Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so check your vendor for updated packages.
  • PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Some distributions and LTS vendors provide backported fixes, so contact your vendor for details, or upgrade to a supported version.
  • Given the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, PHP 8.0, and PHP 8.1 to help people building from source or without access to an LTS vendor.

If you cannot update immediately: while only an update is a complete solution, the following measures reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe.

RCE via OOM corruption (CVE-2026-109618):

  • Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.
  • Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.
  • Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

RCE via stale global state (CVE-2026-109619):

  • Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.
  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.
  • Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors or @ does not help.
  • Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing and cleanup.

The advisories linked above have the full technical details.

item.title: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE in PHP (426 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce, See on Hacker News

Executive Summary

  • Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them. 

  • PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.

  • These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, putting every affected website in immediate risk. 

  • Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.

  • On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.

  • These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability  required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.

Overview

In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.

Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.

PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.

Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.

We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Google, Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel, and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.

The Vulnerabilities

All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. The applications listed below are targets we chose for the RCE demonstrations. They are representative targets - exploitation does not require one of these CMSs, as the vulnerable code is in PHP itself.

Tracking IDBugWhat an attacker can achieveWhat we demonstrated
CVE-2026-109618

Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

Remote process-memory disclosure

Corrupt process memory and execute code

Unauthenticated disclosure of PHP worker memory

Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla

Application-agnostic remote memory disclosure

CVE-2026-109619

Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

OPcache type confusion

Corrupt process memory and execute code

Corrupt shared PHP state and execute code

Pre-authentication RCE on Drupal

Pre-authentication RCE on WordPress

While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.

Impact

We combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress (wordpress:latest), Drupal (drupal:latest), and Joomla (joomla:latest), using their latest container images at the time of testing.

These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.

Demonstrations of PHP2Shell with Wordpress, Joomla, and Drupal: 

The AI inflection point

The vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale. 

With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. 

We used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.

Using Gemini 4 Argon, the team at Wiz has shown why frontier AI is a game-changer for cyber defense. For over a decade, these critical vulnerabilities remained unaddressed because vulnerability discovery and exploitation were incredibly complex. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them.

Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Industry-level collaborations

Prior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.

A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application. PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.

Technical deep dive

Bug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

PHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize). A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.

On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.

The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.

These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.

Bug: Remote process-memory disclosure

PHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id). An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.

A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start(), making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.

Bug: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

In affected versions, PHP retains the backtrace of the most recent fatal error in EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace). A fatal out-of-memory error can destroy the request heap without undefining that executor-global value. The worker survives with a global that still points to memory from the previous request.

If the same worker emits a diagnostic early in the next request, it can access the pointer before the executor reinitializes that state. PHP then destroys or updates the dangling backtrace and follows attacker-reclaimed memory. The resulting cross-request use-after-free can be developed into controlled memory corruption. We demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against Drupal using this primitive.

Bug: OPcache type confusion

OPcache persists compiled PHP structures in shared memory and assigns indices into per-worker runtime-pointer maps. Workers coordinate those indices through a shared frontier. During zend_accel_script_persist(), PHP advances the process-local CG(map_ptr_last) frontier. It publishes the corresponding shared frontier only after persistence completes. An allocation failure between those two events leaves the process-local advance in place and partially persisted objects referring to slots that the shared state still considers available.

When another worker later reuses one of those slots for a different runtime object, stale shared metadata resolves to a pointer of the wrong type. The mismatch creates a cross-worker type confusion and corrupts shared OPcache state. We used this primitive to build an unauthenticated RCE chain against WordPress.

There are other variants outside of these four bugs. While we initially reported these four to PHP, through this research we realized the vulnerability is deeply rooted in the PHP codebase and will require a comprehensive fix. Other variants should also fold under the same two CVEs.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intel Center advisory for PHP2Shell, which includes built-in coverage for agentless and runtime vulnerability detection, exploitation detection via Wiz Defend and Sensor, and automatic response policies, alongside remediation and threat hunting guidance.

Sensor customers using the newest version (1.0.12768) can also enable a built-in response policy to automatically terminate processes exhibiting behaviors typical of PHP2Shell exploitation:

Conclusion

With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflection point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit. With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. Vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. These same capabilities also give defenders a chance to uncover and fix flaws that have survived years of scrutiny.

Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research, with Argon making a particularly significant contribution to finding and helping to remediate the vulnerability. 

The opportunity is to make this work routine: systematically finding flaws in existing software and catching new ones before they reach production. Our coordinated efforts with PHP, OpenAI and Calif advance that goal, applying AI to strengthen the software foundations we all share.

Responsible disclosure timeline

  • August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.

  • August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.

  • August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.

  • August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.

  • September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.

  • October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.

  • October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

Stay in touch

Hi there! We are Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team (@wiz_io). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io.

item.title: Most advice is right for the person giving it (141 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://coached.com/essays/most-advice-is-right-for-the-person-giving-it/, See on Hacker News

Mentor’s CornerSeptember 5, 2026

About Rohan

Steve Jobs gave a famous speech at Stanford, where he told graduates that the only way to do great work is to love what you do, and that if you haven't found your passion yet, you should keep looking.

Interestingly, Mark Cuban says the opposite: don't follow your passion, follow your effort, because you'll end up loving whatever you get good at.

Who’s right?!

I think they're both right…about themselves. Jobs was obsessive; he only ever did well at things he was obsessed with, so of course that's his rule! Cuban is the kind of person who gets hooked on anything he starts winning at, so that's his.

A lot of advice is like this. Two smart people can tell you opposite things, and both can make perfect sense.

So how do you work out what actually applies to you?

Does this apply to me?

Take another common contradiction which contains good advice on each side: “say yes to everything” versus “say no to almost everything.” If your career has gone a bit quiet - you're not getting many opportunities, you're not trying new things, or you're early in your career - saying yes more is likely excellent advice.

If you already have ten things going on and can’t give any of them enough attention, the exact opposite is probably better. Engineers see this all the time. One team writes about how microservices saved them, another writes about moving back to a monolith, and each was right for its own team size and problems.

When you hear advice or someone tells you to do something: don’t copy the rule, understand why it worked for that person. What problem were they solving? What was true about their situation?

Then ask the obvious question: is that true for me too? Don’t assume something that works for someone else is what you’ll enjoy too.

Side note: That’s also why I think finding out your wiring is super important. The better you understand how you naturally work, what gives you energy, how you make decisions, and what kinds of environments bring out your best, the easier it is to tell when someone else’s advice actually fits you and when it doesn’t.

To find out your wiring, take the ~3 minute personality assessment that maps a lot of this for you. It’s built on decades of psychology research, and goes much deeper than the usual four-letter personality stuff.

Take the test - it's free

Or enter coached.com/quiz in your browser.

Start with the boring answer

When I’m confused by a lot of different directions, I love to ask: what’s the boring, obvious answer here?

Take weight loss. You can spend months debating keto, fasting, meal timing, carbs, exercise routines, etc. But what's the boring answer? Eat less. Everyone already knows this. That's what makes it boring.

Which is why I find it pretty funny that Ozempic is arguably the biggest weight-loss breakthrough in decades - and all it does is make you…eat less. Billions in R&D, and the answer was the platitude the whole time. Ha.

I find this useful whenever I’m stuck. What’s the simplest answer here? Am I actually doing that? Why not? There's a well-known essay among programmers called "Choose Boring Technology" that makes the same argument for picking tools.

Boring advice gets ignored because there’s a whole industry built on advice, and the obvious doesn’t sell :) The older I get, the more I realize the boring platitudes are often the best advice.

Can I just find out?

Here's a habit I've ingrained in myself. You're going to have a lot of people telling you what you should do: do this, try that, you have to be doing X.

Instead of taking their word for it or ignoring it, I step back and ask: can I just find out for myself? Can I run a small experiment and get my own answer?

Quick example: a lot of content creators say (no surprise) that creating content is the best thing you can do for your career. I could see it working for them, especially for job searching. I just didn't know if it was worth it for me. So I tested it: posted on LinkedIn consistently, grew a decent following, and paid attention to what it actually did for me. My answer: useful, but not useful enough to keep putting the same energy into it. So I'm less active there now and I don’t wonder about it anymore.

Get into the habit of testing things out in a small way first! If you’re thinking of switching careers, do a small paid gig at a reduced rate first. If you want to build a company, use AI to make a prototype first and try to market it.

Before making any big decision, ask: what could I do that would give me actual data?

We trust confident people, even when they're wrong

The human brain has a pathetic flaw: we routinely mistake confidence for competence.

This is proven in the research too. There’s a 2013 study where people rated statements made with high confidence as far more credible, even when the speaker was demonstrably wrong and had no evidence to back it up.

When someone speaks with absolute conviction on a podcast or in a boardroom, your own instincts wobble. "They sound so sure. Maybe my read is completely backward."

Train yourself to develop an immune response to charismatic certainty. When someone speaks with zero nuance, try to mentally discount their certainty and look at the actual argument underneath. What do they actually know? What evidence do they have?

Use AI to argue the other side

AI can make almost any position sound convincing. Ask whether you should quit your job and it can make a great case for leaving. Ask why you should stay and it can make a great case for that too. A Stanford study published in Science this year found chatbots agreed with people asking for personal advice about 49% more often than humans did.

So I find it more useful as a sparring partner than an oracle. If I’m leaning one way, I’ll ask it to make a case for the opposite, point out what I might be assuming, and tell me what information would change the answer. It helps me stay grounded and make up my own mind!

From Coached Weekly, issue 368.

I also send these out by email.
